```{r}
#Setting the working directory
setwd("/Users/joe/Desktop/Masters Program/Fall 2026/Fundamentals of Machine Learning/Module 8/Assignment 5")

#Reading in the csv to create the original data frame
OriginalCereal <- read.csv("Cereals.csv")
```

```{r}
#chunk for installing or calling packages needed for work
library(dplyr)
  #install.packages("cluster")
library(cluster)
  #install.packages("tibble")
library(tibble)
library(mclust)
  #install.packages("mclust")
```

```{r}
#Chunk for cleaning and transforming data

#removing rows with blank values per the assignment instructions
CleanCereal <- OriginalCereal %>%
  filter(complete.cases(.))

#Since the clusters are being used to find a healthy cluster of cereals, I can remove some columns/variables that are less valuable for us
#for example, shelf, type & mfr are not as valuable

TrimmedCereal <- CleanCereal %>%
  select(-mfr, -type, -shelf)

#Need to standardize/scale numeric values
ScaledCereal <- TrimmedCereal %>%
  mutate(across(-c(name), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))
ScaledCereal <- ScaledCereal %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  column_to_rownames(var = names(ScaledCereal)[1])

head(ScaledCereal,5)
```

```{r}
#Apply hierarchical clustering to the data using Euclidean distance to the normalized measurements

#dissimilarity matrix
d <- dist(ScaledCereal, method = "euclidean")

#hierarchical clustering using complete linkage
hc1 <- hclust(d, method = "complete")

#plot dendrogram
plot(hc1, cex = 0.4, hang = -1)
```

```{r}
# Compute with agnes and with different linkage methods
hc_sngl <- agnes(ScaledCereal, method = "single")
hc_comp <- agnes(ScaledCereal, method = "complete")
hc_avg <- agnes(ScaledCereal, method = "average")
hc_ward <- agnes(ScaledCereal, method = "ward")

#compare agglom coeff with different linkage methods
print(hc_comp$ac)
print(hc_avg$ac)
print(hc_sngl$ac)
print(hc_ward$ac)
```

```{r}
#using ward linkage and euclidean distance

# ward linkage with euclidean distance
hc_ward <- agnes(ScaledCereal, metric = "euclidean", method = "ward")

# dendrogram plot
pltree(hc_ward, cex = 0.4, hang = -1, main = "Dendrogram of AGNES (Ward)")
rect.hclust(hc_ward, k = 5, border = 1:4)
```
I chose k=5, with a height of ~10 as the cutoff point because of the structure of the dendrogram. There are pretty long verticals before these 5 groups are subdivided.


```{r}
#going to check the stability of the clusters at k=5
hc_full <- agnes(ScaledCereal, metric = "euclidean", method = "ward")
cl_full <- cutree(as.hclust(hc_full), k = 5)
table(cl_full)   # cluster sizes

#partition and cluster partition A
set.seed(404)
n <- nrow(ScaledCereal)
idx_A <- sample(n, size = round(0.6 * n))

A <- ScaledCereal[idx_A, ]
B <- ScaledCereal[-idx_A, ]

hc_A <- agnes(A, metric = "euclidean", method = "ward")
cl_A <- cutree(as.hclust(hc_A), k = 5)

# centriods- one row per cluster
cent <- as.matrix(aggregate(A, by = list(Cluster = cl_A), FUN = mean)[, -1])

# Assign each row of B to the closest centroid
B_mat <- as.matrix(B)
assign_B <- apply(B_mat, 1, function(x) which.min(colSums((t(cent) - x)^2)))

full_B <- cl_full[-idx_A]    # full-data clusters for the same B records

# cross tab to show centroid based assignment vs full-data cluster
tab <- table(Partition_A_centroids = assign_B, Full_data = full_B)
tab

#adjusted random indexing
library(mclust)
adjustedRandIndex(assign_B, full_B)

#% agreement after matching labels
sum(apply(tab, 1, max)) / sum(tab)

stab <- sapply(1:20, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  idx <- sample(n, round(0.6 * n))
  cl <- cutree(as.hclust(agnes(ScaledCereal[idx, ], method = "ward")), k = 5)
  cent <- as.matrix(aggregate(ScaledCereal[idx, ], by = list(cl), FUN = mean)[, -1])
  asg <- apply(as.matrix(ScaledCereal[-idx, ]), 1,
               function(x) which.min(colSums((t(cent) - x)^2)))
  adjustedRandIndex(asg, cl_full[-idx])
})
summary(stab)

```

The clusters are somewhat stable, not super stable, but given the task at hand, and not wanting to include the 3 products that are off in their own tiny cluster in one of the larger clusters, especially due to the height of their breaking in the dnedrogram, I am going to stick with 5 clusters, recognizing that some trade-offs were made here.

```{r}
FinalCerealCluster <- CleanCereal %>%
  mutate(Cluster = cl_full)

FinalClusterAvg <- FinalCerealCluster %>%
  group_by(Cluster) %>%
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), 2)))
```

After looking across the clusters, I would suggest cluster #4. This cluster has a decent, or middling, amount of protein compared to other clusters, lower fats and sugars than most other cereal groups, and the highest amount of vitamins on average.
